title: Adjectives and adverbs
tagline: Order, feeling vs cause, how extreme, and exactly where the adverb goes.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 3 — word formation
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Speaking Part 1 — giving full, natural answers with accurate description
why: Getting adjectives and adverbs slightly wrong doesn't confuse a listener, but it does make you sound like you're translating: a red small bag instead of a small red bag, or I'm boring when you mean I'm bored. B2 First checks these patterns in word formation and transformations, and examiners notice them immediately in speaking and writing.

diagrams.title: The order adjectives go in before a noun
diagrams.caption: a beautiful, small, old, round, red, Peruvian, wooden table

rows.label: Describes
cells: what something is like — the cause of the feeling

rows.label: Example
cells: Liam was bored during the revision session.

rows.label: Common mistake
cells: 'I'm boring' when you mean you feel bored
'the film was bored' when you mean it caused boredom

rows.label: Meaning
cells: can exist in degrees — more or less of it
already at an extreme or absolute point

rows.label: Example
cells: very tired, really interesting, quite good
absolutely exhausted, completely convinced, totally amazing

rows.label: Watch out
cells: 'absolutely good' sounds wrong — good is gradable
'very exhausted' is common in speech, but absolutely/completely is more precise

formula.chip: adverb of manner: end of clause

head: Pattern
Rule
Example
rows: a beautiful small old round red Peruvian wooden table
Sofia felt frustrated with the results.
before the main verb; after the verb 'be'
She often checks her notes. She is often late.
usually at the start, followed by a comma
Honestly, I didn't expect to win.

use.point: Putting adjectives in the right order before a noun

examples.text: Nadia bought a beautiful old leather backpack at the market in Cusco.
Mateo's small round glasses steamed up as soon as he walked into the café.

use.point: -ed for how you feel, -ing for what causes the feeling

examples.text: Sofia felt frustrated when her code kept crashing the night before the deadline.
Liam looked embarrassed after mixing up the dates for the trip.

use.point: Choosing the right intensifier for gradable and ungradable adjectives

examples.text: I was really nervous before the mock speaking exam.
By the final whistle, the whole team was absolutely exhausted.
Miss Vega seemed completely convinced the new format would work.

use.point: Where adverbs go, and the confusable pairs hard/hardly, late/lately

examples.text: Nadia hardly ever misses a training session, even in the rainy season.
He answered every question confidently, even the ones he wasn't sure about.
Honestly, I didn't expect the coast trip to be cancelled.
examples.note: sentence adverb, comment on the whole sentence

examples.text: Liam trained hard all summer, but by Saturday's match he could hardly stand.
examples.note: hard = with effort; hardly = almost not

watch_out.wrong: She has a big beautiful house.
watch_out.why: Opinion adjectives (beautiful) come before all other categories, including size.

watch_out.wrong: I'm so boring in this class.
watch_out.why: -ed describes how the person feels; -ing describes what causes the feeling.
Good is gradable, so it pairs with very/really/quite, not with absolutely.

watch_out.wrong: Liam runs very hardly to catch the bus every morning.
watch_out.right: Liam runs really hard to catch the bus every morning.
watch_out.why: Hard (adverb) means 'with effort'; hardly means 'almost not' — 'very hardly' doesn't exist.
Late means 'not on time' or 'at a late hour'; lately means 'recently' — completely different meanings.
A verb needs an adverb, not an adjective, to describe how the action happens.

dialogue.title: Rehearsal notes
dialogue.context: Sofia, Liam and Nadia are reviewing their first rehearsal for the school talent show, and Miss Vega joins to give feedback.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: That was actually pretty impressive for a first rehearsal, wasn't it?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I don't know, I felt genuinely embarrassed during the dance part.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Come on, it wasn't that bad. You just need to move more confidently.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Easy for you to say. You've got that beautiful old guitar and you barely even rehearse.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: That's because she hardly ever needs to — she's already really good.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Not true. I practised hard all week, actually.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Can I interrupt? Honestly, the whole routine looked far better than last year's.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Really? Because from where I was standing, it looked pretty chaotic.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: It was a little chaotic, yes, but the ending was absolutely brilliant.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: See? We just need one more really focused rehearsal before Friday.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Agreed. And Liam, maybe borrow Sofia's small round sunglasses for the final pose.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Fine, but only if nobody laughs.

items.sentence: Sofia has a ___ backpack she bought in Cusco.
items.why: the correct order is size before colour before material

items.sentence: I was ___ when the results came out.
The documentary about the Amazon was genuinely ___.
items.why: -ing describes what causes the feeling — the documentary itself

items.sentence: After the final match, the players were ___ exhausted.
items.why: exhausted is an extreme adjective, so it pairs with absolutely, not very/quite

items.sentence: Nadia is ___ late for training — she's always the first to arrive.
items.why: hardly ever = almost never, an adverb of frequency

items.sentence: Liam answered the interview questions really ___.
items.why: an adverb is needed to modify the verb 'answered'

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct form of the word in brackets.

items.sentence: Liam felt really ___ (EMBARRASS) after tripping on stage.
The trek up to the ruins was ___ (EXHAUST), but absolutely worth it.
Nadia was ___ (AMAZE) when she got the scholarship.
Mateo gave a genuinely ___ (SURPRISE) answer in class today.
By the end of the marathon, all the runners looked completely ___ (EXHAUST).
The team played surprisingly ___ (GOOD) in the second half.

items.first: Sofia's trainers are red, small and made of leather.
The film made everyone in the cinema feel very bored.
items.second_start: Everyone in the cinema found the film

items.first: Liam trains with a lot of effort every single day.
I haven't had any news from Mateo in recent days.
The whole performance was really amazing from start to finish.

summary: Adjectives before a noun follow a fixed order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.
-ed adjectives describe how someone feels; -ing adjectives describe what causes that feeling.
Gradable adjectives (tired, good) take very/really/quite; ungradable ones (exhausted, amazing) take absolutely/completely.
Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb but after 'be'; adverbs of manner usually go at the end.
Don't confuse hard with hardly, or late with lately — they look similar but mean very different things.
